claims.text: Electrochemical dealloying of a multiphase noble metal–based HEA precursor can produce a three-dimensional nanoframework.
Electrochemical dealloying selectively dissolves less-noble elements from the HEA precursor.
Selective dissolution leaves a noble-metal-enriched, interconnected porous structure.
The resulting nanoframework has enhanced catalytic properties.
The proposed precursor is a bulk noble metal–based HEA containing catalytically active noble metals such as Au or Pt and selectively removable less-noble elements.
The HEA precursor is to be electrochemically dealloyed in an acidic electrolyte under controlled potential conditions.
Ambient-temperature treatment in an acid such as HNO3 or HClO4 with controlled potential cycling can selectively dissolve the less-noble components.
Dealloying forms an interconnected three-dimensional nanoporous framework whose remaining ligaments are enriched in noble metals.
Preferential removal of less-stable, less-noble elements creates nanoscale porosity.
Preferential removal of less-noble elements enriches the surface in catalytically active noble-metal sites.
High-entropy stabilization helps the selectively dissolved material maintain a robust phase structure.
The dealloyed three-dimensional nanoframework will have a higher specific surface area than the non-dealloyed bulk HEA.
The dealloyed nanoframework will provide improved electron-transport pathways.
Higher specific surface area and improved electron transport will enhance catalytic activity relative to the as-synthesized, non-dealloyed HEA.
Successful nanoframework formation may depend on uniform elemental distribution in the precursor and precise control of dealloying conditions.
Incomplete removal of less-noble elements or uncontrolled pore formation may limit catalytic enhancement.
The optimal potential, electrolyte composition, and dealloying duration remain undetermined.
The long-term stability of the nanoframework under catalytic operating conditions remains undetermined.
